books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1. Public domain.
stimulus.text: That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States... shall... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands...

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1, public domain
stem: The Homestead Act is best understood as part of which broader development of the 1860s?

options.text: Federal promotion of westward settlement through land grants.
The end of all federal involvement in the West.
options.misconception: The act is federal involvement; the government gave away its own land to settlers.

options.text: The restriction of western migration to the Atlantic coast.
options.misconception: The act pulled settlers westward onto public land, not back to the Atlantic coast.

options.text: The sale of western land only to the highest bidder.
options.misconception: Homesteaders paid a small $10 filing fee and earned the land by living on it, not by outbidding others.

rationales.A: The Homestead Act of 1862, the Morrill Land-Grant Act, and the Pacific Railway Act all used federal land to push settlement and development west. Background: the Morrill Act granted 30,000 acres per member of Congress for agricultural colleges.
rationales.B: The act is the federal government acting in the West, giving away public land on purpose.
rationales.C: The act offered land in the West; it pulled people westward, not eastward.
rationales.D: A homesteader paid a $10 fee and earned the patent by five years of residence and cultivation, not by bidding.
rationales.general:
1. Place the act in its year. Congress passed it in May 1862, in the middle of the Civil War.
2. Look at its neighbors. The same Congress passed the Morrill Act for farm colleges and the Pacific Railway Act for a railroad.
3. Name the pattern. Three laws, one idea: use federal land to fill and develop the West.
Remember: laws travel in packs. When one Congress passes three land laws in one summer, read them as one program.
